name: Rafael Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the marketing at Calloway's Biscuits, a family firm that's been baking in the same town for ninety years. There's me, my boss Graham, and an agency we use for the adverts. I write the packet copy, plan the Christmas tins campaign, and look after the shops and the local paper. Some days I'm out at the factory taking photos of the shortbread coming off the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. Mr Calloway still walks the floor every morning, and when I write that the recipe hasn't changed since 1936, it's true. What wears me out is being told by the agency that we need to be on every new app. I don't use AI, and I've no plans to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good honest work wins in the end. At church I'd probably joke that the robots didn't come after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means Calloway's carries on and so do I. Hannah and I have a good deposit saved for a house and our wedding is paid for. I'm well paid for a small firm, and if it came to it, there are other food companies round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd push Graham to put more into the Christmas tins, because that's half our year. And I'd keep putting money toward the house, hoping to buy in the spring after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Like the weather's settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you at Calloway's, regardless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets squeeze us on price every year. And Mr Calloway (the owner) is 71, and nobody knows what his children will do with the biscuit firm. That's the real worry, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to stop sending me articles about AI. Then I'd ask them to do the job we pay them for, which is the Christmas advert.

say: I'd say **good honest work** wins in the end.
I'd joke at **church** that the robots never came.
think: Calloway's **carries on** and so do I.
Our **house deposit** is saved and the wedding is paid for.
do: Push Graham to spend more on the **Christmas tins** campaign.
Keep saving to **buy a house** after the wedding.
Carry on writing **packet copy** without AI.
S0.quote: Mr Calloway (the owner) is 71, and nobody knows what his children will do with the biscuit firm. That's the real worry, not computers.
fieldNote: His real worry is **family succession** at the firm, not AI.
Money is **secure**, with deposit and wedding covered.
He values work that is **true**, like the 1936 recipe.

steps.text: Push for a bigger Christmas tins campaign at Calloway's
Keep saving toward a house deposit with Hannah

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one sounds more likely than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still buy from people, and a biscuit firm needs someone who knows the town. I'd say it loud, because I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. If the agency starts offering cheap AI copy and plans, Graham might decide he doesn't need me as well as them. I'm the one who doesn't use the tools, so I'm the easy saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and make myself useful in ways a computer can't, like the shop visits and the town fete stand. I'd save harder, maybe another two hundred a month. And I'd hold off on the house until I knew my job was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Unsettled, like someone's moved the furniture in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people buy from people. So why hold off on the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because what I believe and what Graham's accountant believes might be different. I'd rather be wrong and safe than right and stuck with a mortgage. Hannah would agree, she's more careful than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the tools if Graham asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he asked, I'd do it, because he's my boss. I wouldn't like it. But I'd rather do it his way than not have a job.

say: I'd say **people buy from people**, and a biscuit firm needs locals.
I'd say it **loud**, because I believe it.
think: The agency's **cheap AI copy** could make me look unnecessary.
Not using the tools makes me the **easy saving**.
do: Do more **shop visits** and the town fete stand.
Put the **house purchase** on hold until the job feels safe.
feel: **Unsettled**, like someone moved the furniture in the dark.
S1.quote: I'd rather be wrong and safe than right and stuck with a mortgage.
fieldNote: His public faith in **people** sits beside private fear for his job.
He'd learn AI only **if his boss asked**.
Delaying the house shows **caution** over conviction.

steps.text: Do more Calloway's shop visits and run the town fete stand
Hold off buying a house with Hannah until the job is safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before our first anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this was done to us by a few tech companies without anyone asking. At work I'd say we should stick together, and online I'd probably say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone. Everything I do, writing, planning, the newsletter, a machine does better. Mr Calloway would be loyal, but loyalty doesn't pay wages when the supermarkets want cheaper biscuits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad straight away. He runs a building supplies yard on the ring road, and he's always said there's a place for me. That's hands-on, selling timber and loading vans, so the robots are three years behind. Hannah and I would push the house back and live smaller, and I'd keep every penny of the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. And angry, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you angry at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who built it and rushed it out. And partly myself, for thinking a nice family firm would protect me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would going to your dad's yard feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humbling. I went to university so I wouldn't have to load vans at my dad's timber yard. But it's honest work and it's family, and I'd rather that than a handout.

say: I'd say a few **tech companies** did this without asking anyone.
At work I'd say we should **stick together**.
think: My **job's gone**, because a machine does everything I do better.
**Loyalty** from Mr Calloway doesn't pay wages.
do: Ask Dad for a job at his **building supplies** yard.
Push the **house purchase** back and live smaller.
Keep every penny of the **deposit** untouched.
S2.quote: I went to university so I wouldn't have to load vans at my dad's timber yard. But it's honest work and it's family, and I'd rather that than a handout.
fieldNote: He blames **tech firms** and partly himself.
Falls back on **family**, not the state, as his values predict.
His father's **hands-on yard** buys a few years before robots.

steps.text: Ask his dad for work at the building supplies yard
Leave Calloway's marketing for selling timber and loading vans
Push back the house purchase with Hannah
Keep the whole house deposit in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to protect family firms and local jobs, and I'd vote for whoever says that, whatever party they're from. I'd still say people buy from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd see it coming and still not want to move. I know myself. But I'd be 32, maybe with a baby, and I can't be the man who saw it coming and did nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start working Saturdays at my dad's yard to learn the trade side, the stock, the builders, the orders. I'd stay at Calloway's while it lasts. And Hannah and I would still buy a house, but a small one, with a mortgage her teaching wage could carry alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. Like I've got a rope to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a baby. Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd still have children. My grandparents had kids in harder times than this. A smart machine won't stop Hannah (his fiancée) and me having children. It might mean a smaller house and fewer holidays, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Saturdays at the yard, not a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I trust learning by doing more than a course. Dad learned from his dad. That's how it's always worked in our family.

I'd **vote** for whoever says that, whatever party they're from.
think: Five years means I'd see it coming and still **not want to move**.
I can't be the man who **did nothing**.
do: Work **Saturdays** at Dad's yard to learn the trade.
Buy a **small house** Hannah's wage could carry alone.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, with a rope to hold.
S3.quote: My grandparents had kids in harder times than this. A smart machine won't stop Hannah (his fiancée) and me having children.
fieldNote: He knows his **resistance** and plans around it.
**Family plans** stay firm, with a smaller house.
Prefers **learning by doing** at the family yard to a course.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at his dad's building supplies yard
Vote for candidates who back family firms and local jobs
Buy a small house on a mortgage Hannah's wage covers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so let's not panic or throw money at it. I'd say firms should train their own people instead of firing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably leave it too late. I'd be 37. I'd keep telling myself next year. But my writing job still ends in the end, I don't kid myself about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham if Calloway's would put me through some sales training, so I'm closer to the shops and the buyers. I'd keep saving and we'd buy the house next year. In five years I'd decide between the yard and staying, and I'd make Hannah hold me to that date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a worry I'd keep pushing down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like things as they are. I've been at Calloway's five years and I'd stay forty if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade and good manners. Something with their hands, and the sense to treat people right. I'm not sure a marketing degree is worth it anymore. I'd want my children to learn a trade and good manners.

Firms should **train their own people**, not fire them.
think: Ten years is long enough that I'd **leave it too late**.
My **writing job** still ends; I don't kid myself.
do: Ask Graham for **sales training** paid by Calloway's.
Buy the **house** next year and keep saving.
Set a **five-year date** to choose between the yard and staying.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a worry I keep pushing down.
S4.quote: I'm not sure a marketing degree is worth it anymore. I'd want my children to learn a trade and good manners.
fieldNote: He predicts his own **delay** and builds in a deadline.

Doubts his **own degree** for his future children.

steps.text: Ask Calloway's to pay for sales training this year
Buy a house with Hannah next year
Keep saving every month toward a cushion

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't have time to change and I know I'm slow to change. What would help is employers being made to give real notice and train people, and family firms like Calloway's getting some protection against the big companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith and community. When things go wrong, it's church and family people turn to, not an app. I'd want those things still standing at the end of all this.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, it's church and family people turn to, not an app.
portrait: Rafael, 27, does the marketing at **Calloway's Biscuits**, a ninety-year-old family firm, and never uses AI.
He's engaged to Hannah, a teacher, with a **house deposit** saved and wedding paid.
In Steady Disruption he fears being **the easy saving** and holds off buying a house.
In AGI by 2028 he'd go to his **dad's building yard**, choosing family over a handout.
With more time he plans slowly but knows he may **leave it too late**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he's slow to change and would have no time.
whatWouldHelp: Real **notice and training** from employers, and protection for family firms.
